The best video annotation tools for object tracking support frame interpolation, timeline editing, and persistent object IDs. These features reduce manual work and improve consistency, which is key for image recognition tasks. Tools built for image annotation don’t always scale to long video sequences or complex object tracking. Label Your Data offers a data annotation platform built for teams working on object tracking, segmentation, and video classification tasks. CVAT is an open-source video annotation tool built for teams that want full control over object tracking workflows. It supports video labeling with frame-by-frame tracking, interpolation, and object ID management. V7 Darwin is a commercial video annotation tool built around deep learning workflows, with support for object tracking, segmentation, and multi-class labeling. Frame-by-frame annotation is available, featuring interpolation and persistent object IDs. This is complemented by built-in model-assisted tools like Auto-Annotate and support for Segment Anything (SAM). Teams can train and deploy models inside the platform to assist labeling, and use automation features like object re-identification across frames. SuperAnnotate is a full-stack annotation platform with strong QA workflows and support for video object tracking. It includes timeline-based labeling with frame interpolation and object ID tracking, plus tools for multi-annotator consensus and reviewer scoring. The platform integrates with custom models for pre-labeling and supports long video sequences, though real-time collaboration may be slower on high-frame-count projects. It handles long sequences well and supports timeline-based editing, interpolation, and persistent object IDs. The platform includes version control, QA workflows, and collaborative features. Kili Technology supports video labeling with core features like frame interpolation, timeline editing, and object ID assignment. Dataloop is a cloud-based data engine with integrated video annotation tools, model hosting, and QA workflows. If your team’s already labeling in-house, one of the best video annotation tools can give you full control. Video data annotation means adding labels to objects in video frames. Look for tools that support automatic interpolation, object linking, and persistent IDs. These features let you label an object once and have it track across frames, saving hours on long videos.

I need to calculate inter-rater agreement (2 annotators) on a small dataset (let's say 10 items), where annotators used between 1 and 4 labels per item. Based on everything I've read, Krippendorff's alpha seems to be the thing I should use, but I can't figure out how to use it with multi-label data instead of single-label data. How can I measure inter-rater agreement with multi-label data? ## 1 Answer 1. First one is how to calculate agreement in case of multi-label annotation. The second one is what function to use, in R or in a different language, to do this calculation. The answer to first question is that you should:. Here is explained how to calculate Krippendorff's alpha for multi-label annotation using MASI distance using Python. from nltk.metrics import masi_distance. task_data = [('coder1','Item0',frozenset(['l1','l2'])),. I have not found any implementation Krippendorff's alpha in R that lets you use custom distance function as nltk.metrics.agreement does. The solution is to use irrCAC library, as it's krippen.alpha function accepts the weight matrix as argument. Than, one can calculate the weight matrix for all observed combination of labels using any distance function. I call python to calculate MASI distance. dataset <- data.frame(matrix(dataset,ncol = 2, byrow = T), stringsAsFactors = F). #function that calculates MASI distance using python nltk.metrics. masi <- function(x,y,split = " "). if(length(str_split(x,split,simplify = F)) == 1). x <- str_split(x,split,simplify = F). x <- unlist(str_split(x,split,simplify = F)). if(length(str_split(y,split,simplify = F)) == 1). y <- str_split(y,split,simplify = F). y <- unlist(str_split(y,split,simplify = F)). masiD <- nltk$masi_distance(pybuiltins$set(x),pybuiltins$set(y)). #calculating weight matrix for all observed combination of lables using MASI distance. krippen.alpha.raw(dataset, weights = distMasi,categ.labels = rownames(distMasi)). ## Your Answer.
